note.title: Volodimer Vsevolodovič
note.p: Volodimer Vsevolodovič, son of Vsevolod M′stislavič, provides another example of siblings marrying siblings. The next entry details the marriage of his sister Verxoslava to Bolesław IV of Poland, but Volodimer was himself to marry Boleslaw’s elder sister Richeza. Richeza had previously been married to Magnus Nielsson of Denmark, Knýtlinga Saga, 130. The Knýtlinga Saga records that they had two children, Knud and Nicholas, but whether they followed their mother or stayed in Denmark is unknown. Knud, however, is there years later and becomes king. Incidentally Magnus was the cousin and murderer of Knud Lavard (ibid., 134–35), husband of Ingeborg M´stislavna. See above for Ingeborg M´stislavna. but after Magnus’s death in 1134 Magnus was killed by Eric Emune, brother of Knud Lavard, and husband of Malfrid discussed above. Ibid., 139. she remarried. In 1135, Richeza married Volodimer Vsevolodovič, presumably as part of her father, Bolesław III’s, attempt to increase his ties with the M´stislaviči. Volodimer died not long after their marriage, in 1139, and Richeza remarried again, this time to Swerker I, king of Sweden. Ibid., 151.

While there is much to say about Richeza, her marriages, and her children that is substantiated by quite a few primary sources, the identity of Volodimer Vsevolodovič is mostly an educated guess. This hypothesis of identification is subscribed to by many, including Baumgarten, Balzer, and more recently Nazarenko. Baumgarten, “Généalogies,” table 5; Balzer, Genealogia Piastów, 150–51; Nazarenko, Drevnjaja Rus´ na meždunarodnyx putjax, 582. There is a rival school of thought, however—the two biggest proponents of which seem to be J. Gallén and E. A. Rydzevskaja, J. Gallén, “Vem var Valdemar den stores drottning Sofia?” Historisk Tidskrift för Finland 61 (1976): 273–88; and E. A. Rydzevskaja, “Drevnjaja Rus´ i Skandinavija v IX–XIV vv.: Materialy i issledovanija,” Drevneišie gosudarstva na territorii SSSR 1978 (1978): 8–236. though I first came across it in the work of Litvina and Uspenskij, as well as that of N. I. Ščaveleva6 J. Gallén, “Vem var Valdemar den stores drottning Sofia?” Historisk Tidskrift för Finland 61 (1976): 273–88; and E. A. Rydzevskaja, “Drevnjaja Rus´ i Skandinavija v IX–XIV vv.: Materialy i issledovanija,” Drevneišie gosudarstva na territorii SSSR 1978 (1978): 8–236. — that the proper identification for Richeza’s Rusian husband is Volodar´ Glěbovič, ruler of Minsk. The argument, as put forward by Ščaveleva for the identification of Valadar (the name from the Scandinavian sources) as Volodar´ Glěbovič, is that during the later twelfth century there was a battle between Volodimerko Volodarič (son of Volodar´ Glěbovič of Minsk) and Vasil´ko Jaropolčič (grandson of Izjaslav M´stislavič of Kyiv) over Bereste, and the Volodariči (Volodimerko’s brother, also named Vasil´ko) got involved as they were able to utilize Polish connections to stymie their opponents. Ščaveleva, Drevnjaja Rus´ v “Pol´skoj istorii” Jana Dlugoša, 435. 8. Tatiščev, Istorija Rossiiskaja, vol. 2, s.a. 1077. 9. Ščaveleva, “Pol´ki—zheny russkix knjazej (XI–seredina XIII v.),” 56n42 However, the argument is not entirely convincing, only in part because Tatiščev is the main source for the battle and the terminology for the Polish kinship ties. Tatiščev, Istorija Rossiiskaja, vol. 2, s.a. 1077. Tatiščev’s kinship ties are occasionally dubious and thus not always reliable, but moreover the argument for the relationship between the families is confused and confusing and once again has no solid basis in primary sources. The final nail in the coffin is that Volodar´ Glěbovič did not die until 1159, thus giving Richeza no reason to leave Rus´ and marry Swerker of Sweden in 1139. Ščaveleva, “Pol´ki—zheny russkix knjazej (XI–seredina XIII v.),” 56n42.

This debate between the two sides effectively illustrates the problem that exists when there is little or no primary source information. The only primary sources to mention the name Volodimer Vsevolodovič are a few Rusian chronicles that briefly mention his role in freeing his father from Novgorod in 1136. NPL, s.a. 1136, for example. The source for Richeza’s Rusian husband comes in two Scandinavian sources, Knýtlinga Saga and Fagrskinna, which record the same basic information. Richeza was married to a Valadar, king of so-called Polinalande, which is often translated as Poland. Knýtlinga Saga, 242; and Finnur Jónsson, ed., Fagrskinna, Nóregs kononga tal (Copenhagen: S. L. Møllers Bogtrykkeri, 1902–1903), 300. For translation as Poland, see Knýtlinga Saga, 150. However, following Peter Sawyer, we can make the assumption that Poland is not meant, but rather the land of the Poljanians, especially since a similar remark is made in Adam of Bremen for Rus´, and thus bring the problem back to one of which Rusian it was she married. Peter Sawyer, Kings and Vikings: Scandinavia and Europe, AD 700–1100 (London and New York: Methuen, 1982), 141; for the remark in Adam of Bremen, see Adami gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum, ed. J. M. Lappenberg, Scriptores rerum germanicarum in usum scholarum ex Monumentis Germaniae historicis recusi (Hannoverae: Impensis Biblipolii Hahniani, 1876), bk. 3, ch. xv.14. The identity of Richeza’s second husband is mentioned in these sagas because her daughter with Valadar, Sofija, For more on Sofija, see N. de Baumgarten, “Sofija russkaja, koroleva datskaja, a zatem landgrafinja tjuringenskaja,” Seminarium Kondakovianum 4 (1931): 95–104.
married Valdemar of Denmark at the instigation of Richeza’s son in Denmark, King Knud. Of additional interest, as Nazarenko points out, if Valadar is Volodimer Vsevolodovič, then the marriage is consanguineous, though that may not have been a burning concern for them, as it was neither the first nor the last consanguineous marriage in Rusian history. Nazarenko, Drevnjaja Rus´ na meždunarodnyx putjax, 582. The problem of the identity of Valadar of Polinalande remains, and is relatively insoluble due to the lack of adequate primary sources.

Having stipulated this, the identification of Valadar as Volodimer Vsevolodovič is tentatively accepted because the marriage of Richeza and a M´stislaviči makes good political sense, which seems to be the underlying motivation for many if not all of these dynastic marriages. A marriage between the two would have strengthened the ties between Bolesław III, who was ruling at the time, and the Monomaxoviči, who were ruling in Kyiv. Such a marriage between a Polack ruler of Minsk, such as Volodar´ Glěbovič, makes much less sense in terms of the large-scale politics in which Bolesław III participated.
